text: A large network has more than enough parameters to memorise its training data, including its noise and accidents. When that happens, training error keeps falling while error on new examples starts to rise, and the network has learned the examples rather than the pattern. Part of the problem is that neurons can come to rely on very particular partners, forming fragile arrangements that only work on data they have already seen.

Dropout, introduced by Geoffrey Hinton's group around 2012, attacks this directly. During training, at every step, each neuron's output is switched off with some probability, say one in ten, chosen independently and afresh each time, and the rest of the network has to produce a good answer without it. It is like a team in which any colleague might be absent on any given day: nobody can depend on one particular person, so knowledge has to be spread around and duplicated.

There is one piece of bookkeeping. If a tenth of the outputs are zeroed, the next layer receives a smaller total than it would with everyone present. The standard fix, called inverted dropout, divides the surviving outputs by the probability of survival during training, so the expected total stays the same. At test time dropout is switched off entirely, every neuron takes part, and no rescaling is needed.

There is a lovely way to see what dropout does. Every random mask picks out a different thinned network, and there are astronomically many of them, all sharing the same weights. Training with dropout trains this whole family at once, and running the full network at test time behaves roughly like averaging all of their predictions, which is a classic way of reducing overfitting.

You can see the effect in the loss curves. With dropout, training loss is a little higher, because the network always works with a handicap, but the gap between training and validation loss narrows, and validation loss often ends lower. Dropout is one regulariser among several, alongside weight decay, early stopping and simply collecting more data, and they are often used together.

The original transformer applied dropout with a rate of one in ten, and so did the first GPT. Some of today's largest language models, trained on so much text that they rarely see the same example twice, use little or no dropout during pre-training, because with that much data memorisation is less of a threat, but it remains common when fine-tuning on smaller datasets.

So dropout randomly silences neurons during training, forcing the network to spread what it knows, and steps aside at test time. That completes our tour of neural networks; next we begin training in practice, starting with tensors and batches.
